stemMd: According to the passage, which objection to street-by-street canopy targets is becoming less forceful?
instructionsMd: Answer on the basis of the passage only.

options.label: A
options.textMd: That maintenance budgets are often the first to be cut

options.label: B
options.textMd: That such targets are expensive to monitor

options.label: C
options.textMd: That saplings take fifteen to twenty years to cast meaningful shade

options.label: D
options.textMd: That trees in narrow streets need costly soil cells to survive

explanationMd:
Find the sentence that lists the critics' objections. The third paragraph gives two: street-level targets "are expensive to monitor", and trees in narrow streets "need costly soil cells". It then says "the first is weakening", and explains why: block-level satellite temperature data is now available at almost no cost.

The first objection is the monitoring cost, so that is the one losing force.

**How to check.** "The first" refers back to the first item in the list just given. The satellite explanation confirms it: cheap data answers a monitoring objection, not a planting-cost one.

distractorRationale.d: This is the critics' second objection. The passage calls it fair and says nothing to weaken it; cheap satellite data does not make soil cells cheaper.
distractorRationale.c: The time saplings take to grow is the author's own "deeper difficulty" in the last paragraph, not one of the critics' objections to street-level targets, and the passage does not say it is weakening.
distractorRationale.a: Maintenance budgets come up in the last paragraph as part of the author's point about time. They are not presented as an objection to street-level targets.

accessibilityText: A question about the passage on urban tree-canopy targets. It asks which objection to street-by-street targets the passage says is becoming less forceful. The four options are: expensive to monitor; narrow-street trees need costly soil cells; saplings take fifteen to twenty years to give shade; maintenance budgets are often cut first.

provenance.notes: Original item testing a back-reference ("the first"). Distractors are the other objection and two points from a different paragraph.

review.author: bocconi-graduate-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: Paragraph 3: critics say street-level targets are expensive to monitor and need soil cells; 'the first is weakening' because satellite data is cheap. The first objection is cost of monitoring = B. D is the second objection (not said to weaken). A and C come from paragraph 4 and are not objections to street-level targets.
